back: Using electrolysis to coat an object with a thin layer of a metal.
To improve appearance and to improve resistance to corrosion (often using little of an expensive metal).
Object = cathode; plating metal = anode; electrolyte contains ions of the plating metal.

front: Why clean an object before plating?
back: Grease, dirt or rust stop the metal coat sticking evenly.

front: Why does the electrolyte concentration stay constant in plating?
back: Metal ions removed at the cathode are replaced at the same rate by the dissolving anode.

front: Copper purification: anode, cathode and electrolyte
back: Anode: impure copper. Cathode: pure copper. Electrolyte: acidified copper(II) sulfate solution.
Anode: Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻. Cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
Unreactive metals (silver, gold, platinum) that fall from the anode; a valuable by-product.

front: What happens to zinc and iron impurities in copper refining?
back: They dissolve and stay in solution as ions; they are not deposited on the cathode.

front: Uses of copper and the property behind each
back: Wiring (conductor, ductile); pipes (resists corrosion); pans (thermal conductor); brass and bronze alloys.

front: Percentage of copper in a used anode
back: Mass gained by the cathode ÷ mass lost by the anode × 100.
